Bulky Molecules Tailor Solvent Packing Fraction of Electrolytes for High‐Voltage Sodium‐Ion Battery
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT High‐voltage sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) suffer from rapid degradation caused by electrolyte oxidation and interfacial parasitic reactions, which are strongly influenced by the local solvation environment near the electrode surface. However, conventional electrolyte design focuses on tuning Na + –solvent interactions while overlooking solvent packing within the solvation shell. Herein, we reveal that a bulky molecular solvent mediates restricted solvent packing around Na + , with its reduced packing efficiency quantitatively described by the fractal dimension ( D f ). The enlarged molecular volume creates a more open solvation environment, facilitating anion participation and promoting ion clusters dominated by contact ion pairs (CIPs) and small aggregates (SAGGs). The resulting inorganic‐rich interphase suppresses electrolyte oxidation and interfacial parasitic reactions, enabling stable high‐voltage operation. Sodium iron sulfate (NFS) paired with the bulky‐solvent electrolyte retains 80% capacity over 1407 cycles at 1 C. An Ah‐level HC||NFS pouch cell retains 81.53% capacity after 500 cycles. A practical pouch cell further achieves 115.05 Wh kg −1 and retains 80.87% of its capacity after 150 cycles. This work demonstrates that restricted solvent packing can modulate ion association and interfacial chemistry, providing a molecular design consideration for high‐energy SIBs.

papers.title: Molecular Design of Fluorinated Ester Electrolytes via Skeleton Regulation Enables Aggressive Cathode Chemistries in 5V‐Class Fast‐Charging Lithium‐Ion Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Lithium‐ion batteries can deliver higher energy densities when using high‐voltage cathodes such as LiNi 0.5 Mn 1.5 O 4 (LNMO), yet their practical application is hindered by the catalytic nature of high‐voltage cathode materials which usually cause electrolytes decomposition. Although the utilization of fluorinated carbonates as electrolyte solvent considerably inhibited the parasitic reaction at cathode side, the irrational fluorination often leads to the sluggish Li + transport which finally causes poor rate performance. Here, we design a family of trifluoromethyl‐substituted carboxylate esters as electrolyte solvents. We found that the spatial arrangement between the ‐CF 3 and the carbonyl group in these fluorinated esters is critical for regulating the electrolyte solvation structures. A short distance (α‐substitution) severely weakens the solvating power of the solvent, resulting in a substantial decrease in ionic conductivity, whereas an extended separation (γ‐substitution) compromises the oxidation resistance against high‐voltage cathodes. Only the trifluoromethylation at the β‐position yields optimal solvent (methyl 3,3,3‐trifluoropropionate, MTFP) that can simultaneously meets high‐voltage and fast‐charging requirements of LNMO||Gr cells when pairing with fluoroethylene carbonate and 1 M LiPF 6 . In such electrolyte, the Ah‐level LNMO||Gr pouch cells deliver 78% capacity retention at 6C charge/discharge rate (13.2 mA cm −2 ), and stably operate over 300 cycles at the high rate of 3C.

papers.title: From Carrier Behavior to Cathode Design: Toward High‐Performance Aluminum Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT This review systematically summarizes recent advances in cathode materials for aluminum batteries (ABs), emphasizing the critical influence of carrier properties on electrode performance. Focusing on carrier properties, including ionic size, valence, charge density, and coordination environment, we analyze their transport kinetics, interfacial reactions, and energy storage mechanisms across different cathode systems, including Al 3+ , AlCl 4 − , AlCl 2 + , as well as the synergistic behavior of multiple carriers. We identify intrinsic carrier characteristics, solvation/desolvation dynamics, and the electrode/electrolyte interface as the primary factors governing battery performance. Furthermore, the review delineates the constraints of cathode materials in achieving high capacity, fast kinetics, and long‐term cycling stability. An integrated framework for understanding carrier behavior and energy storage mechanisms is established, accompanied by a systematic classification of cathode materials, including inorganic, Prussian blue, and organic compounds, together with their corresponding optimization strategies. Finally, universal design principles for structural engineering, electronic structure modulation, defect/doping, and interface engineering are proposed. More importantly, this review establishes a carrier‐centered framework that systematically links carrier chemistry, charge storage mechanisms, and cathode design principles, thereby providing a unified mechanistic perspective for the rational development of next‐generation high‐performance ABs.

papers.title: Engineering the Ir─O─Ni Interface Bonds in Ir@Ni‐MOF to Accelerate Li 2 O 2 Formation and Decomposition for High‐Reversibility Li‐O 2 Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Aprotic lithium‐oxygen (Li‐O 2 ) batteries have attracted considerable interest due to their ultrahigh theoretical energy density, yet their practical application is severely limited by slow cathode reaction kinetics and large voltage hysteresis. Here, we report an interface engineering strategy to construct ultrafine Ir nanoparticles anchored on Ni‐based metal‐organic framework (Ir@Ni‐MOF) as an efficient bifunctional cathode catalyst for Li‐O 2 batteries. Experimental and theoretical calculations reveal the formation of interfacial Ir─O─Ni chemical bonds, inducing significant charge redistribution and downshifting the d‐band center of Ir@Ni‐MOF. This electronic modulation weakens the adsorption affinity toward the LiO 2 intermediate, thereby enhancing a solution‐mediated discharge pathway to form nanosheet‐like Li 2 O 2 with intimate interface contact and rapid charge/mass transfer, which facilitates reversible decomposition during charging. As a result, the Ir@Ni‐MOF cathode delivers a remarkably low overpotential of 0.76 V, an extended cycling stability over 400 cycles at 500 mA g −1 , outperforming most reported MOF‐based and noble‐metal catalysts. This work provides a promising avenue for designing high‐performance Li‐O 2 batteries and beyond through precise electronic structure engineering.

papers.title: Crystallography‐Dependent Plating/Stripping Kinetics and Interfacial Morphologies in Zn Metal Anodes
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Crystallographic orientation governs Zn deposition, dissolution, and cycling stability, but its influence on interfacial charge‐transfer kinetics remains difficult to quantify. Here, scanning electrochemical cell microscopy coupled with fast scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) is used to resolve Zn plating and stripping on single‐crystal (002), (100), and (101) surfaces. Meniscus‐confined measurements reveal facet‐dependent branch‐specific apparent zero‐current potentials and apparent exchange current densities, j 0 , with the kinetic ordering j 0 (100) > j 0 (101) > j 0 (002) for both plating and stripping. This ordering is reproduced across independently prepared electrodes and retained over different scan rates and aqueous electrolytes. Beyond charge transfer, Zn removal and regrowth are strongly crystallographically encoded: dissolution footprints preserve the symmetry of the parent facets, while potentiostatically deposited Zn adopts substrate‐dependent growth geometries. These coupled kinetic and morphological differences translate directly to battery performance. Despite its slower apparent kinetics, the close‐packed, low‐energy (002) facet exhibits the longest cycling life in Zn/Zn symmetric cells and substantially improved capacity retention in both polyaniline/Zn and Na 0.33 V 2 O 5 /Zn full cells, whereas the faster (100) and (101) interfaces fail earlier. These findings establish a facet‐dependent kinetics–stability trade‐off and show that durable Zn anodes require coordinated control of charge transfer, dissolution topology, and crystallographic reconstruction.

papers.title: Cross‐Phase Impurity–Interphase Regulation for Suppressing Thermally Accelerated Failure in Ni‐Rich Pouch Lithium‐Ion Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Practical LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 ||graphite pouch cells suffer rapid degradation under thermal stress because liquid‐phase impurity reactions, electrode interphase failure, and cathode–anode cross‐talk are tightly coupled. However, most strategies are designed to address either impurity chemistry or interphase chemistry, leaving the amplified cross‐talk between electrolyte degradation and electrode failure unresolved. Here, we propose a cross‐phase impurity–interphase regulation strategy using p‐Phenylenebis(dimethylvinylsilane) (PDVS) for LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 ||graphite pouch cells. The vinyl‐dimethylsilyl groups endow PDVS with synchronized liquid‐phase scavenging and solid‐phase interphase‐forming capability. In the liquid phase, PDVS acts as an impurity scavenger, lowering HF from 90.88 ppm to 29.44 ppm while reducing residual H 2 O from 10.65 to 8.45 ppm, thereby suppressing LiPF 6 hydrolysis and reducing the accumulation of corrosive by‐products. At the solid interfaces, PDVS preferentially participates in interfacial reactions to construct Si‐containing cathode‐electrolyte interphase and solid‐electrolyte interphase on the Ni‐rich cathode and graphite anode, mitigating electrolyte decomposition, gas evolution, transition‐metal crossover, and resistance growth. Consequently, 2 Ah LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 ||graphite pouch cells retain 92.81% capacity after 304 cycles at 45°C, show reduced swelling during 60°C storage, and maintain 86.5% capacity after over 1620 cycles at 25°C. This work establishes cross‐phase impurity–interphase regulation as a manufacturing‐compatible electrolyte design principle for thermally durable Ni‐rich pouch cells.

papers.title: Rest‐Pulse Interphase Reconstruction Enables Capacity Recovery in Aged Lithium‐Ion Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT To address capacity loss associated with inactive Li‐related species and solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) growth, we developed a Rest‐Pulse (RP) protocol for aged LiFePO 4 /graphite diagnostic pouch cells. The protocol combines a 12 h discharged‐state rest with a short voltage pulse. The rest step partially dissolves and restructures the graphite‐side SEI, reducing interfacial blocking. Quantitative ex situ 7 Li solid‐state nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR) shows a pronounced decrease in NMR‐detectable residual metallic Li after RP treatment. Atomistic molecular‐dynamics simulations further indicate that the pulse produces a short‐range, field‐dependent directional bias of isolated Li‐rich domains within the porous interphase rather than long‐range migration. The RP protocol achieves a 99.3% average Coulombic efficiency and ∼10% absolute capacity recovery, exceeding the recovery obtained from rest alone (∼6%). A coupled recovery process occurs involving SEI reconstruction, improved interfacial kinetics, and changes in inactive Li‐related inventory. The RP protocol provides a proof‐of‐concept route for non‐destructive capacity recovery, although larger‐format validation and chemistry‐specific optimization are still required.

papers.title: Rational Solvent Fluorination Design for Solvation Regulation Enabling Stable Interfaces in High‐Voltage Li‐Ion Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Fluorinating electrolyte solvents is an effective strategy to enhance the interfacial stability of lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs) under high‐voltage conditions, where severe interfacial side reactions typically undermine the long‐term performance. However, the influence of both the number and positional arrangement of fluorinated groups on solvation structure remains poorly understood. In this work, we systematically investigate how trifluoromethyl group number and substitution position in diethyl carbonate (DEC) derivatives affect Li + solvation behavior. It is revealed that the introduction of a DEC‐based solvent with symmetric two trifluoromethyl groups tends to regulate the solvation structure enriched with anions and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC). This optimized solvation structure facilitates the formation of a robust cathode‐electrolyte interphase derived from both anions and FEC. Consequently, Ni‐rich LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 cathodes with a high loading mass of 10.5 mg cm −2 achieve stable cycling at 4.6 V, retaining 80% of their capacity after 300 cycles. These findings provide fresh insights into the rational design of fluorinated solvents for high‐voltage LIBs.

papers.title: Empirical Understanding of Li‐Ion Transport Through Hetero‐Grain Boundaries Within Li‐Electrolyte Interface for Stable Li Metal Anodes
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Understanding the Li‐ion transport mechanism across the Li/electrolyte interface (LEI) is fundamental for stabilizing Li‐metal batteries (LMBs). In particular, hetero‐grain boundaries (h‐GBs) such as Li 2 O/LiF or Li 2 CO 3 /LiF are theoretically recognized to provide favorable Li‐ion pathways within inorganic LEI; however, experimental verification of h‐GB‐mediated Li‐ion transport remains elusive. In this study, we provide experimental evidence for favorable Li‐ion transport associated with h‐GBs using a tailored h‐GB‐rich MgO/MgF 2 heterostructure (MgO/F). Multifaceted analyses indicate that the MgO/MgF 2 heterointerfaces establish a favorable Li‐ion transport environment through coupled interfacial effects, with the enhanced defect population potentially contributing to increased Li‐ion carrier availability. Furthermore, upon contact between the Li substrate and the MgO/F layer acting as the LEI, the MgO/F layer spontaneously constructs a dual‐interfacial architecture: an inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphase abundant in h‐GB‐rich Li 2 O/LiF and a Li/substrate interphase consisting of a Li–Mg alloy with rapid Li surface migration. This synergistic interfacial architecture maximizes the practical efficacy of h‐GB‐rich MgO/F for stabilizing Li metal anodes. Consequently, the h‐GB‐rich MgO/F demonstrates exceptional electrochemical stability, significantly outperforming bare Li in both symmetric and full cells. This study provides experimental insight into the role of h‐GBs in inorganic interfaces and provides a strategic blueprint for designing highly stable LMBs.

papers.title: Breaking the Additive Paradox in Aqueous Aluminum‐Ion Batteries via Weak‐Coordination Asymmetric Electrolyte Chemistry
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Aqueous aluminum‐ion batteries (AAIBs) are compelling for sustainable storage, yet the strong hydrolysis of Al 3+ acidifies the electrolyte, causing corrosion and passivation that necessitate modification. Additives designed to break the rigid Al 3+ solvation shell face a paradox: they often compromise reversibility via either dielectric collapse or kinetic deadlocks. Here, we break this paradox by establishing a weak‐coordination asymmetric electrolyte based on aluminum trifluoromethanesulfonate (Al(OTF) 3 ), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC). DMSO coordinates to Al 3+ , displacing coordinated water to suppress water activity, but cannot preserve the dielectric environment. FEC compensates via three synergistic functions: high dielectric constant for electrostatic screening, weak hydrogen bonding for solvation asymmetry reinforcement, and reductive decomposition for solid electrolyte interphase(SEI) formation. The sequential coupling of DMSO‐mediated solvation disruption with FEC‐enables dielectric/interfacial compensation accelerates desolvation and stabilizes electrode: a fluorinated SEI enables 2000 h reversible Al plating/stripping, while a spinel‐to‐layer transformation creates a fluorinated interface on vanadium oxide with asymmetric channels, mitigating dissolution. The full cell retains 90.8% capacity after 2000 cycles at 4 A g −1 . By showing that resolving one bottleneck can expose another, this work reframes additive optimization as sequential processes of identifying and compensating coupled failure mechanisms, generalizing a design principle for multivalent aqueous electrolytes.

papers.title: Unlocking the Interfacial Activity of Insoluble Lithium Salts for Stable Lithium Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Employing functional lithium salts in electrolytes is an effective strategy to suppress anode instabilities and sluggish charge‐transfer kinetics in lithium batteries. However, high solubility requirements intrinsically exclude a broad class of promising, high‐lattice‐energy inorganic salts for carbonate electrolytes. Here, we establish an immobilized functional platform (IFP) by deploying insoluble lithium salts with strong Lewis‐acidic Li + sites directly onto an aramid‐scaffolded separator. This design bypasses conventional dissolution–diffusion limitations, yielding a thin, ionically conductive, LiF‐rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) driven by regulated interfacial Li + solvation and enhanced anion‐derived decomposition. Systematic screening and 6 Li/ 7 Li isotope tracing identify Li 2 SO 4 (LS) as the optimal IFP candidate (IFP‐LS) owing to its moderate Lewis acidity, superior solvent affinity, and industrial viability. Remarkably, LS provides a finite sacrificial lithium contribution during continuous SEI evolution, mitigating irreversible lithium consumption. Consequently, IFP‐LS separators quadruple the lifespan of Li||LiNi 0.9 Co 0.05 Mn 0.05 O 2 cells at 0.7 C compared to bare separators, and deliver 88.4% capacity retention over 2400 cycles in Li||LiFePO 4 cells at 5 C. Scalability is further validated through 100 m roll‐to‐roll manufacturing across diverse Ah‐level formats, adding only 0.163 USD m −2 . This work overcomes the lithium salt solubility barrier and unlocks a vast library of potent materials for next‐generation high‐energy‐density batteries.

papers.title: Pre‐Intercalated Cation Optimizing Proton Topochemistry for High‐Performance Aqueous Zinc‐Ion Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Cation pre‐intercalated oxides have been widely explored as cathode materials for aqueous zinc‐ion batteries (AZIBs). Although the influence of intercalants on the material structure and Zn 2+ storage capacity has been adequately studied, an in‐depth understanding of the influence of intercalants on proton storage is still lacking. Especially, proton transport exhibits ultrafast kinetics as an ideal charge carrier, playing a crucial role in the performance of AZIBs. We show that pre‐intercalated K + in K 0.5 V 6 O 13 (KVO) not only reinforces the [VO] framework but also optimizes the hydrogen‐bonded network composed of confined lattice water, achieving ultrafast proton transport. Benefiting from the optimization of proton topochemistry, the capacity, rate performance, and cycling stability of KVO improve significantly. KVO delivers a high reversible capacity of 462.9 mAh g −1 at 0.2 A g −1 and 82.3% retention after 20000 cycles at 20 A g −1 . Even with the high mass loading of 19.2 mg cm −2 , a KVO||Zn pouch cell with 539.2 mAh capacity can achieve stable cycling for more than 300 cycles at 0.5 A g −1 . This work provides new insights into how pre‐intercalated cations affect the proton topochemistry and electrochemical performance of inorganic cathodes.

papers.title: Pore‐Stitching Engineering of Biomass‐Derived Hard Carbon for Enhanced Sodium‐Ion Storage
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Biomass‐derived hard carbon (HC) is a promising and cost‐effective anode for sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). Prior to carbonization, biomass precursors are commonly subjected to acid/alkali purification to remove metallic and non‐metallic impurities. However, the accompanying ionic etching process often generates abundant through‐pores and disrupts the carbon framework, leading to increased irreversible capacity loss. Herein, we propose a “pore stitching” strategy using hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC) as a functional reconstruction precursor. The hydroxyl‐rich HEC is proposed to interact with oxygen‐containing sites in the demineralized precursor and to be retained within accessible pore regions during mixing and drying. During subsequent carbonization, HEC‐derived carbon contributes to the reconstruction of the disrupted carbon framework, resulting in reduced open surface exposure and a redistributed micro/ultramicroporous architecture while preserving favorable Na + storage domains. Consequently, the optimized HC delivers a high reversible capacity of 375.3 mAh g − 1 at 20 mA g − 1 . A 700 mAh pouch cell pairing this HC with sodium iron phosphate pyrophosphate (Na 4 Fe 3 (PO 4 ) 2 P 2 O 7 , NFPP) delivers 150 Wh kg − 1 based on the combined active‐material mass of both electrodes and retains 97.8% capacity after 200 cycles at 1 C. This work provides a viable route for converting impurity‐rich agricultural waste into high‐performance HC anodes for practical sodium‐ion energy storage.

papers.title: Performance of a 5 V-Class Thin-Film Li Battery at a High Current Density of ∼30 mA cm–2
papers.abstract_en: All-solid-state Li batteries operating at high current densities exceeding 10 mA cm-2 are desired for high-power and rapid-charging batteries. Therefore, battery development needs to focus on reducing the electrolyte-electrode interface resistance at high current density, which is a major contributor to internal resistance. However, methods for reducing the electrolyte-electrode interfacial resistance at high current densities remain unexplored. Here, we demonstrate charge-discharge operation at 30 mA cm-2 using Li3PS4, LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4, and Li metal as a solid electrolyte, 5 V-class positive electrode, and negative electrode, respectively. The introduction of Li3PO4 buffer layers at both Li-Li3PS4 and Li3PS4-LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 interfaces reduced the interfacial resistance 45,000-fold. Furthermore, the introduction of a 5 nm-thick Pt layer instead of Li3PO4 at the Li-Li3PS4 interface enabled charge-discharge operation under high-current-density conditions. This quantitative study highlights the importance of designing electrochemically robust negative electrode and electrolyte interfaces for high-power 5 V-class all-solid-state Li batteries.

papers.title: Multifunctional and Near Zero‐Strain Li‐Rich In‐Li Intermetallic Anodes for Stable Cycling of Li‐S Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Li‐S batteries (LSBs) are emerging as formidable contenders in the field of energy storage systems, owing to their cost‐effectiveness and ultrahigh energy density that surpasses that of conventional Li‐ion batteries. Nonetheless, unresolved issues, such as Li dendrite growth and parasitic chemical reactions between the Li metal and dissolved polysulfides, pose significant safety concerns and remain major hurdles to their commercial viability. Herein, we propose a Li‐rich In 3 Li 13 intermetallic alloy anode (In‐Li IMA) fabricated via a simple roll‐pressing and pressure‐holding process. Unlike previous studies that focused primarily on stabilized interfaces for dendrite suppression, the in situ‐formed In‐Li IMA demonstrates not only significantly inhibited dendritic Li growth but also minimized volume change during cycling, owing to its ionically and electronically conductive 3D framework. Furthermore, simulation studies reveal that the In‐Li IMA suppresses polysulfide‐induced side reactions due to its hole‐dominated conduction and weaker polysulfide adsorption energy relative to Li. In contrast to the control Li cell that exhibits significant capacity fading, the In‐Li IMA cell achieves 87.4% capacity retention over 600 cycles and exhibits improved cyclability even in large‐area pouch‐cell configurations. Based on this accessible approach for fabricating large‐scale multifunctional anodes, this study provides critical design insights for developing practical anodes for LSBs.

papers.title: Microstructure Evolution in Dry‑Coated Sulfidic All‐Solid‐State Battery Cathodes: Investigating Core–Shell Particle Morphology
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT This study investigates continuous extruder mixing and high‑shear batch mixing to promote the formation of core–shell‐like particle coatings for enhanced interfacial contact in dry‑coated sulfidic all‑solid‑state battery cathodes containing 82 wt.% high‐Ni NCM85 (LiNi 0.85 Co 0.10 Mn 0.05 O 2 , particle size D 50 3.8 µm) cathode active material and 0.5 wt.% polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) binder. Particle morphology and electrode microstructure are analyzed by particle size measurements, electron microscopy, and X‐ray characterization. Morphological observations indicate that extrusion yields a robust PTFE fibril network and a more homogeneous electrode surface, where deformed Li 6 PS 5 Cl solid electrolyte particles suggest a core–shell‐like coating. Batch mixing resulted in reduced electrode quality, tensile strength, and microstructure homogeneity. Despite its dedicated mechanofusion process and higher specific mechanical energy input (∼ speed, time), a distinct core–shell‐like coating is not evident for such a small‐particle system. Charge transport features are analyzed in symmetric cells under blocking conditions. Batch‑mixed electrodes attain higher electronic conductivity, whereas extruder‑mixed electrodes achieve higher ionic conductivity. These differences likely arise from microstructural features. Electrochemical characterization of half‑cells demonstrates the enhanced performance of extruder‑mixed electrodes, including higher active material utilization, reduced overpotentials, and improved rate capability. Overall, extruder mixing provides a scalable and effective route for engineering the electrode microstructure.

papers.title: Machine‐Learning‐Guided Dopant‐Class Design Enables Near‐Zero‐Strain P2‐Type Cathodes for High‐Voltage Sodium‐Ion Batteries
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Manganese‐based layered oxides are promising cathodes for sodium‐ion batteries, yet their practical deployment is restricted by Mn 3+ ‐induced Jahn‐Teller distortion, irreversible high‐voltage P2‐O2 phase transitions, and oxygen‐related side reactions that collectively cause structural deterioration and rapid capacity fading. Here, based on literature‐correlation analysis of reported Ni─Mn P2‐type cathodes, we establish a machine‐learning‐guided dopant‐class design strategy. The analysis reveals distinct roles of metal, non‐metal, and metalloid dopants in governing cycling stability and redox reversibility, identifying metalloid regulation as the most favorable direction for enhancing high‐voltage structural and redox stability. Guided by this insight, an Al─B─F co‐doped P2‐type cathode is rationally designed, in which boron reinforces the oxygen framework through strong B─O covalency, while Al and F provide complementary cationic and anionic regulation. The optimized cathode delivers 142.8 mAh g −1 at a high average voltage of 3.53 V and exhibits superior low‐temperature capacity retention of 98.19% after 300 cycles at −5 C. In situ XRD, soft x‐ray absorption spectroscopy, ex situ XPS, operando DEMS, and DFT calculations reveal a highly reversible reaction pathway featuring stabilized oxygen redox and near‐zero volumetric strain (ΔV/V ≈ 0.025%). This work establishes machine‐learning‐guided dopant‐class design as a general strategy for developing durable high‐voltage layered sodium‐ion cathodes.

papers.title: Controlled Presodiation of Sodium‐Ion Cathode via Electron Cloud Engineering
papers.abstract_en: ABSTRACT Chemical presodiation offers a promising pathway to compensate sodium deficiency in cathode and anode materials, thereby enhancing the usable energy density of sodium‐ion batteries. This approach is particularly critical for P2‐ and tunnel‐type cathodes, such as Na 0.44 MnO 2 , where the as‐synthesized materials typically exhibit a 50%–60% sodium deficiency. However, conventional presodiation reagents possess excessively high reductive potential, often leading to oversodiation, structural degradation, and compromised electrode reversibility. Here, we report a rational electron‐cloud engineering strategy to precisely control the sodium chemical potential of presodiation agents. Guided by Hückel's rule, we demonstrate that tailoring π‐conjugation size and introducing electron‐withdrawing groups enables the adjustment of sodium chemical potential via a balance of conjugative and inductive effects. We identify 1‐indanone as an optimal presodiation reagent, capable of delivering sodium to Na 0.44 MnO 2 cathodes without any oversodiation. The resulting electrodes exhibit fully restored sodium inventories, an unprecedented first‐cycle Coulombic efficiency of ∼100%, and improved capacity retention over 350 cycles compared to untreated controls. Our findings establish a versatile framework for controlling sodium delivery in chemical presodiation, providing a new avenue for the design of next‐generation sodium‐ion batteries with enhanced stability and performance.
